$comment: The six words this application shows for the state of a person's work, and the whole mapping from an internal state to the wording a person reads for it. One file, because two files drift. It is a linted surface twice over: the `desktop-status-catalog` entry in `tools/program/vocab-lint/surfaces.json` checks every value at `$.states.*.status` against the six approved words, and `desktop-strings-json` checks every string here for the nine terms a person must never meet. `src/app/status.test.ts` checks this file against sections 4.1 and 4.3 of `docs/product-prd.md`, in both directions, so an internal state that gains a row in the product model and no wording here fails the desktop build rather than reaching a person as a fallback label.
$statesComment: Section 4.3 of the product requirements: user-facing status is exactly these six words, in this order. `means` is what the status tells a person; `nextStep` is what they can do about it. A concept that needs a seventh word is a question for the product owner, never a local addition — the lint rejects a seventh value here before anyone can ship it.

states.means: An actor is changing files right now.
states.nextStep: Nothing is needed from you. Open it to read along.

states.means: Their work survived; nobody else has it.
states.nextStep: Nothing is needed from you. It is on this device and it will still be here after a restart.
Anyone on the team can open it. It is not in the shared version yet.

states.means: There is an exact change waiting for a person.
states.nextStep: Read it and approve it, or send it back with what you want changed.

states.means: A human decision is required before this can proceed.
states.nextStep: Open it and decide. Nothing was discarded and nothing was guessed.

states.means: It is in the shared version.
states.nextStep: Nothing is needed from you. Everyone works from it now.

$internalStatesComment: Section 4.1 of the product requirements: every internal state, and the only wording this application may show for it. Four of these wordings are status words and four name a thing rather than a state, which is why this list is longer than the six. The internal names are written here — and nowhere else in the application — precisely so that showing one is impossible without passing through this mapping first: `src/app/status.ts` looks a name up and throws when it cannot find it, and it never puts the name it failed on into a sentence.
